\chapter{The Subjunctive --- the Mood of the Not-Yet-Real}
\label{ch:subjunctive}
\hlchaptermodality{35}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can distinguish an asserted event from a wanted one and use the learned singular present-subjunctive forms after quiero que or ojalá.}

Complete ES-C18-practice and choose asserted versus wanted meaning before retrieving the singular forms of hablar, comer, vivir, querer, poder, and hacer in the two learned trigger frames.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[Hablas español · Quiero que hables español]{Hablas español · Quiero que hables español — fact or wanted event?}

\label{lesson:ES-C18-quiero-que}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Hablas español} can assert “You speak Spanish.” Now compare \textbf{Quiero que hables español} — “I want you to speak Spanish.” \textbf{Hables} does not report what is true. It presents the speaking as wanted and not yet asserted. That meaning contrast is the first small doorway into the \textbf{subjunctive}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: count the doers}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{meaning} & \textbf{Spanish} & \textbf{doers} \\
\midrule
I want to speak Spanish. & \textbf{Quiero hablar español.} & one: I want; I speak \\
I want you to speak Spanish. & \textbf{Quiero que hables español.} & two: I want; you speak \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

With one doer, keep the known infinitive \textbf{hablar}. With a different doer for the wanted event, use \textbf{que} and the new form \textbf{hables}. This is a bounded pattern for \textbf{querer}, not a rule for every clause in Spanish.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item “Hablas español.”
  \item “Quiero hablar español.”
  \item “Quiero que hables español.”
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which form asserts the event? (\textbf{Hablas.}) Which presents it as wanted? (\textbf{Hables}, after \textbf{quiero que}.) What happens when the wanter and the speaker are the same? (Use the infinitive: \textbf{Quiero hablar}.) Next, build the three singular \textbf{-ar} forms one piece at a time.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hable · hables · hable]{hable · hables · hable — the singular -ar row}

\label{lesson:ES-C18-subjuntivo}



\begin{quote}
You already used \textbf{hables} for one friend. Today add only the other two singular slots:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{person} & \textbf{present subjunctive} \\
\midrule
yo & habl\textbf{e} \\
tú & habl\textbf{es} \\
él / ella / usted & habl\textbf{e} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Plural forms wait. Say the small row: \textbf{hable · hables · hable}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the yo stem, then a vowel swap}]
Start from present \textbf{hablo}. Remove \textbf{-o} to reveal \textbf{habl-}. Regular \textbf{-ar} verbs then use \textbf{e} in these subjunctive endings: \textbf{-e, -es, -e}. The family vowel has swapped from the familiar \textbf{a} to \textbf{e}. This recipe will matter later because a verb's special present \textbf{yo} stem can travel with it.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Spanish \textbf{subjuntivo} descends from Latin \textbf{subiūnctīvus}, “subjoined,” from \textbf{sub-} “under” plus \textbf{iungere} “join.” English \textbf{join}, \textbf{junction}, and \textbf{conjunction} belong to the same word family; \textbf{yoke} is a more distant cousin. The name helps you picture the wanted clause joined under \textbf{quiero que}. It is history, not a complete usage rule.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Build each answer only from the learned singular row.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the three forms. (\textbf{Hable, hables, hable.}) Which present form supplies the stem? (\textbf{Hablo.}) What did the family vowel do? (\textbf{a $\to$ e}.) What does the name remember? (A clause \textbf{subjoined}, or joined under another.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[coma · comas · coma]{coma · comas · coma — let -er cross to a}

\label{lesson:ES-C18-comer-subjuntivo}



\begin{quote}
Start from \textbf{como}, remove \textbf{-o}, and keep \textbf{com-}. A regular \textbf{-er} verb crosses to the \textbf{a} family:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{person} & \textbf{present subjunctive} \\
\midrule
yo & com\textbf{a} \\
tú & com\textbf{as} \\
él / ella / usted & com\textbf{a} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Say only the singular row: \textbf{coma · comas · coma}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: meaning before machinery}]
\textbf{Comes} can assert “you eat.” \textbf{Quiero que comas} presents your eating as what I want. The \textbf{e $\to$ a} contrast helps you hear the two meanings. It does not mean that every \textbf{a} form is subjunctive; use the learned frame as a whole.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Keep \textbf{comer} inside the learned singular frame.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the three forms. (\textbf{Coma, comas, coma.}) Which form asserts “you eat”? (\textbf{Comes.}) Which belongs after \textbf{quiero que}? (\textbf{Comas.}) Next, test whether regular \textbf{-ir} behaves differently.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[viva · vivas · viva]{viva · vivas · viva — -ir joins -er}

\label{lesson:ES-C18-vivir-subjuntivo}



\begin{quote}
Start from \textbf{vivo}, remove \textbf{-o}, then add the same \textbf{a} endings you just used with \textbf{comer}:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{person} & \textbf{present subjunctive} \\
\midrule
yo & viv\textbf{a} \\
tú & viv\textbf{as} \\
él / ella / usted & viv\textbf{a} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Regular \textbf{-er} and \textbf{-ir} match in this singular row:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{comer:} \textbf{coma · comas · coma}.
  \item \textbf{vivir:} \textbf{viva · vivas · viva}.
\end{itemize}

Plural differences wait.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: meaning in a known frame}]
\textbf{Vives en Madrid} asserts where one friend lives. \textbf{Quiero que vivas en Madrid} makes that living a wanted event. Nothing new is being smuggled into the sentence: \textbf{en} and \textbf{Madrid} have appeared in the earlier location frame.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Keep \textbf{vivir} inside the learned singular frame.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the three forms. (\textbf{Viva, vivas, viva.}) Which regular family matches \textbf{-ir} here? (\textbf{-er.}) Which form fits one friend after \textbf{quiero que}? (\textbf{Vivas.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[quiera · quieras · quiera]{quiera · quieras · quiera — keep the change you know}

\label{lesson:ES-C18-querer-subjuntivo}



\begin{quote}
Present \textbf{quiero} already carries the stressed \textbf{e $\to$ ie} change. Remove \textbf{-o} to get \textbf{quier-}, then add the \textbf{-er/-ir} subjunctive endings:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{person} & \textbf{present subjunctive} \\
\midrule
yo & quier\textbf{a} \\
tú & quier\textbf{as} \\
él / ella / usted & quier\textbf{a} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Say only this bounded singular row: \textbf{quiera · quieras · quiera}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one known verb, one inherited stem}]
You are not learning a new list of stem-changing verbs. You are carrying one known change into one known row. \textbf{Quiero que quieras hablar español} means “I want you to want to speak Spanish.” The sentence is deliberately narrow: no new person noun, object, or plural form.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Carry only the known \textbf{quier-} stem into this row.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the three forms. (\textbf{Quiera, quieras, quiera.}) Which old change stays visible? (\textbf{e $\to$ ie.}) Where did the stem come from? (Known \textbf{quiero}, minus \textbf{-o}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pueda · puedas · pueda]{pueda · puedas · pueda — one more known stem change}

\label{lesson:ES-C18-poder-subjuntivo}



\begin{quote}
Present \textbf{puedo} already carries \textbf{o $\to$ ue}. Remove \textbf{-o} to get \textbf{pued-}, then add the same \textbf{a} row:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{person} & \textbf{present subjunctive} \\
\midrule
yo & pued\textbf{a} \\
tú & pued\textbf{as} \\
él / ella / usted & pued\textbf{a} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Say \textbf{pueda · puedas · pueda}. No other \textbf{poder} forms enter today.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: use it immediately}]
\textbf{Quiero que puedas hablar español} means “I want you to be able to speak Spanish.” Every word was already known except the single form \textbf{puedas}. This is the gentle pattern: learn one row, then spend it in the next sentence.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Carry only the known \textbf{pued-} stem into this row.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the three forms. (\textbf{Pueda, puedas, pueda.}) Which old change stays visible? (\textbf{o $\to$ ue.}) Which form addresses one friend after \textbf{quiero que}? (\textbf{Puedas.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[haga · hagas · haga]{haga · hagas · haga — hago lends its stem}

\label{lesson:ES-C18-hacer-subjuntivo}



\begin{quote}
The known present \textbf{yo} form is \textbf{hago}. Remove \textbf{-o} and keep \textbf{hag-}:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{person} & \textbf{present subjunctive} \\
\midrule
yo & hag\textbf{a} \\
tú & hag\textbf{as} \\
él / ella / usted & hag\textbf{a} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Say \textbf{haga · hagas · haga}. Only \textbf{hacer} enters this lesson; other special stems wait for later chapters.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: spend the new form}]
\textbf{Haces café} can assert “you make coffee.” \textbf{Quiero que hagas café} says “I want you to make coffee.” The \textbf{g} is not a fresh exception: it was already in \textbf{hago}, the present form that supplied the stem.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Carry only the known \textbf{hag-} stem into this row.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the three forms. (\textbf{Haga, hagas, haga.}) Where does \textbf{hag-} come from? (Known \textbf{hago}, minus \textbf{-o}.) Say the wanted event. (\textbf{Quiero que hagas café.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ojalá + subjunctive]{ojalá + subjunctive — a wish borrowed through Arabic}

\label{lesson:ES-C18-ojala}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Ojalá hables español} means “I hope you speak Spanish” or “May you speak Spanish.” \textbf{Ojalá} expresses the wish by itself. It needs neither a main verb nor \textbf{que} before the subjunctive. Keep the first frame tiny:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Ojalá + subjunctive}
\end{quote}

That is a usable modern pattern. It does not make the Arabic source phrase new Spanish vocabulary.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
The Real Academia Española records \textbf{ojalá} from Hispanic Arabic \textbf{wa šá lláh}, “and God has willed.” Long contact in al-Andalus carried the expression into Spanish, where its sound and grammatical life changed. You met another Arabic-derived function word in \textbf{hasta}. The historical phrase explains a route; only modern \textbf{ojalá} is available for your Spanish sentences.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Use only modern \textbf{ojalá} as the Spanish trigger.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What follows \textbf{ojalá} in the learned frame? (The \textbf{subjunctive}.) Does it need \textbf{que}? (\textbf{No.}) Which historical language variety carried the word into Spanish? (\textbf{Hispanic Arabic.}) Is the older Arabic phrase usable as new Spanish vocabulary here? (\textbf{No.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — assert the event or want it}

\label{lesson:ES-C18-practice}



\begin{quote}
This checkpoint adds no vocabulary, plural person, object pronoun, or new clause frame. First decide whether the event is asserted or wanted. Then retrieve only the singular rows you learned.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the bounded map}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{verb} & \textbf{yo / él / ella / usted} & \textbf{tú} \\
\midrule
hablar & hable & hables \\
comer & coma & comas \\
vivir & viva & vivas \\
querer & quiera & quieras \\
poder & pueda & puedas \\
hacer & haga & hagas \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The repeated outer form is not a missing row: first- and third-person singular match. Every plural form waits.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: two safe triggers}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Same doer: \textbf{Quiero hablar español.}
  \item Different doer: \textbf{Quiero que hables español.}
  \item Wish by itself: \textbf{Ojalá hables español.}
\end{itemize}

Do not extend these two frames to every emotion, doubt, command, or conjunction yet. More triggers belong in later micro-lessons.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Decide the meaning first; then retrieve only the learned form.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the first meaning choice? (\textbf{Asserted event or wanted event.}) Give the three regular tú forms. (\textbf{Hables, comas, vivas.}) Give the three bounded special tú forms. (\textbf{Quieras, puedas, hagas.}) Name the two safe triggers. (\textbf{Quiero que} for a different doer; \textbf{ojalá} for a wish.) What still waits? (Plural persons, additional irregular verbs, and additional subjunctive triggers.)
\end{tcolorbox}
